page.text:
Next in importance are *De Morgan's laws*, named after the British
mathematician Augustus De Morgan (1806–1871). These laws reveal a
profound duality between conjunction and disjunction mediated by
negation.

De Morgan's laws state that negating a conjunction turns it into a
disjunction of negations, while negating a disjunction turns it into a
conjunction of negations: $$\neg(P \land Q) \iff (\neg P \lor \neg Q)$$
$$\neg(P \lor Q) \iff (\neg P \land \neg Q)$$

The intuitive meaning is direct: to say that 'it is not the case that
both $P$ and $Q$ hold' means that at least one of them must fail;
similarly, to say that 'neither $P$ nor $Q$ holds' means that $P$ fails
and $Q$ fails. These laws appear in every domain of mathematics: in set
theory, as the laws governing complements of unions and intersections
($(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c$), and in predicate calculus, as the
duality between universal and existential quantifiers
($\neg \forall x P(x) \iff \exists x \neg P(x)$).
